title: Many Hands

post.author: u/night_sitter_nunzia
post.title: Our research firm's reports are drafted by a circle of agents. Tuesday's says two people met at a harbour office on 14 March 2024. They have never been in the same country.

blocks.text: I'm the night analyst at Garthwick Research, a small firm that answers clients' questions with written reports. Since the spring the first draft comes from what the partners call the circle. It is six agents, each a model with tools that picks its own next step: one lead agent and five worker agents. I read the drafts overnight; at 07:00 they go to the client on their own.

The circle works in steps. First the lead reads the client's question and splits it into smaller jobs, called subtasks. Then it hands each worker one subtask with a line of instructions. Passing work on like that is called a handoff. The workers search and read at the same time and send their notes back. Last, the lead joins the notes into one report. The partners like the séance joke: many hands on the table, and the message spells itself.

On Tuesday at 23:00 the circle took a question from Wrayholme Ferries: which UK ports have committed money to shore power since 2022, how much, who decided, and which ferry lines will plug in. Shore power lets a ship at its berth, its place at the quay, switch off its engines and run on electricity from the land. Below is the lead's handoff log. Each line shows the time, who handed work to whom, and the one line of instructions sent; the last line is the lead finishing the report.

23:03  lead to worker 1  Find which UK ports have committed money to shore power since 2022.
23:03  lead to worker 2  Find how much each UK port is spending on shore power, and where the money comes from.
23:03  lead to worker 3  Find who decided each UK port's shore power plan, and when.
23:03  lead to worker 4  Find which ferry lines will plug in to shore power.
23:03  lead to worker 5  Find which UK ports have committed money to shore power since 2022.
23:26  lead         report done: 7 claims

At 01:50 I reached paragraph 6: on 14 March 2024 Hilary Sowerby, Inchcombe's harbour master (the official who runs its harbour), met Ragnhild Skjelbred of the Norwegian ferry line Havbrua at the Inchcombe harbour office, and they agreed that Havbrua's ferries would plug in there.
That afternoon Hilary was at her desk in Inchcombe, and Ragnhild was signing papers on a quay in Norway.

blocks.label: tuesday_notes_paragraph6.png

diagram.aria: Two workers' notes feed one paragraph. Worker 3's note: Hilary Sowerby announced Inchcombe's funding at the harbour office on 14 March 2024. Worker 4's note, from Norwegian sources: Ragnhild Skjelbred of Havbrua signed a shore power deal at the Brennvika quay on 14 March 2024. Neither note carries a source. Both go to the lead's merge, which writes paragraph 6: they met at the Inchcombe harbour office on 14 March 2024.

blocks.caption: Drawn from the circle's scratch file. Worker 3's note and worker 4's both say 14 March 2024 and shore power; neither says where it came from or which worker wrote it. Worker 4's eight sources were all Norwegian. Workers 1 and 5 read the same nine sources and wrote the same notes.

blocks.text: The usage page, our model company's record of what we are billed for, has the run in tokens, the small pieces of text a model reads and writes. The lead: 54,000 tokens in, 10,000 out. The workers: 184,000, 152,000, 206,000, 178,000 and 184,000 in; 6,000, 5,000, 7,000, 6,000 and 6,000 out. 958,000 in and 40,000 out is $3.47 at our invoice's rate, $3 a million in and $15 out. On Wednesday I ran the same question through one agent alone: 236,000 in, 14,000 out, $0.92, 58 minutes against the circle's 26. It invented nothing, but it never reached Thurloe port's money or its ferry lines.

I flagged it at 01:50, but the draft went to Wrayholme at 07:00 before Ms Nesbitt, the partner on the account, read my note. She called it back from the client at 09:00 and wants the circle running again tonight. What do I change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing at that table moved the glass on its own. What you have is a multi-agent system: several agents working on one job, each a model going round its own loop of read, decide, act. Your lead agent is the planner, the part that decides how to split the job and who does each piece. Each worker is a sub-agent, an agent started by another agent for one piece of work. It has its own context window, the most text a model can hold at once, so it knows only what its handoff says. The notes the workers send back are the circle's shared notes, the only thing the lead writes from. The lead's last step, joining those notes into a report, is called the merge. Two questions. What did each worker receive, word for word, and what did the client's question say that a worker's line didn't? And who decides what goes into the shared notes, and can you tell from a note which worker wrote it and from what source?

replies.author: u/night_sitter_nunzia
replies.text: Word for word, the five lines in the log. The client's question says UK ports in its first line; three of the lines say UK and worker 4's doesn't. Workers 1 and 5 got the same line. The notes are plain paragraphs that each worker hands back, and the lead pastes them into one scratch file, a working document, and writes from that. No paragraph says which worker wrote it or which page it came from. I only matched them up by searching the scratch file for the date.

comments.author: u/more_hands_quarrell
comments.text: More agents means more coverage. Five is a small circle for a four-part question. Go to eight: each worker gets a narrower slice, less to hold in its head, less room to wander off to Norway. And two workers on the same part isn't waste, it's a second opinion. When two independent agents write the same fact, you can trust it. The big AI companies run research agents in parallel, many at the same time, for exactly this reason: more hands, more ground covered.

replies.author: u/night_sitter_nunzia
replies.text: Ms Nesbitt likes this one. She says tokens, the pieces of text we pay for, are cheap next to an analyst's hour.

comments.author: u/minute_book_tregenza
comments.text: I keep the minutes, the written record of meetings, for Inchcombe's port board, the group that runs the port. On 14 March 2024 Hilary announced the funding from the harbour office at 11:00 and was there the rest of the day; the visitors' book has nobody from Norway on it that year. We've never had a word from Havbrua. Your client's head of strategy has already rung our office asking for a copy of the minutes of that meeting.

replies.author: u/night_sitter_nunzia
replies.text: I'm sorry. The partners' other idea is to let the workers message each other while they work, so worker 3 would have seen worker 4's note before the lead did.

reply.prompt: The circle runs again tonight. What should Garthwick change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Add more worker agents to the circle, so each one covers a narrower slice of the question and nothing gets missed again.
options.part2: Ms Nesbitt set the circle to eight workers and Nunzia reran Tuesday's question. The lead still wrote one line per worker, going round the four parts twice, so every part went to two workers: 4 duplicated subtasks, and 35 sources read twice. Worker 8 got the same line as worker 4, with no UK only, and read Norwegian sources too. The meeting was still in paragraph 6, now from workers 3, 4, 7 and 8, and Ms Nesbitt read four workers as four witnesses. The run cost $5.41, 5.9 times one agent, and still took 26 minutes, because the slowest worker sets the pace.
options.senior: Adding workers multiplies whatever is wrong with the briefs. With one-line handoffs, more workers means more overlap, more tokens and more notes with no source to merge, and two copies of the same search aren't independent evidence. Fix what each worker is told and what it hands back before changing how many there are.

options.text: Give each worker a goal, limits and a note format with sources; the lead keeps the notes; one agent if it won't split.
options.part2: Nunzia rewrote the lead's instructions. Each brief, the instructions that go with a handoff, now has an objective (what to find), limits (UK ports only, January 2022 on, public sources) and an output format, the shape its notes must take: one finding a line, with its source link, date and place. The lead writes one brief per part, so four workers ran and the fifth wasn't started. Tuesday's rerun: 8 claims, none invented, none from outside the UK, no duplicated subtask, 35 sources. Sowerby's announcement and the two ferry lines plugging in at Inchcombe stayed separate claims, each with its link. 770,400 tokens in and 36,400 out, $2.86, still 3.1 times one agent, in 26 minutes, and with both of Thurloe's answers that one agent never reached. On Thursday Wrayholme asked a follow-up: how Inchcombe decided, step by step, one thread with each step resting on the last. Nunzia ran it both ways: the circle $0.72 in 33 minutes, one agent $0.44 in 31, the same 3 claims. The lead now hands that kind of question to one agent.
options.senior: Every handoff is a brief, and a worker knows only what its brief says. Give each one an objective, limits and an output format with a source per finding, keep the shared notes in one place the lead owns, and spend the extra tokens only when the question splits into parts that can be researched apart.

options.text: Let the worker agents message each other directly as they work, so they share findings and catch each other's mistakes early.
options.part2: Nunzia gave every worker a way to message every other and reran Tuesday's question. Each worker read the others' notes as it went: 120,000 more tokens in, 1,078,000 in all, $3.83, 4.2 times one agent, and 31 minutes, because they waited for each other. Worker 3 read worker 4's note about Brennvika, saw the same date, and wrote the meeting into its own notes. Now the meeting wasn't something the lead made at the merge; it was in two workers' notes, and looked confirmed. Workers 1 and 5 saw each other's notes only after both had read the same nine sources.
options.senior: Letting workers talk spreads unchecked notes faster than it catches them, and nobody owns the result. Anthropic's own post says agents aren't yet great at coordinating in real time. Keep the shared notes with the lead, with a source on every finding, so there is one place to check.

options.text: Retire the circle: an analyst writes each report herself, with a single agent as research help, and checks every claim.
options.part2: Nunzia ran Tuesday's question through one agent and wrote the report herself from its notes. One context window, searching one thing after another: 236,000 tokens in and 14,000 out, $0.92, 58 minutes, 21 sources. Nothing was invented, because she checked each claim against its page. But the agent never reached Thurloe's money or its ferry lines, and finding those by hand took her the rest of the night. The report went out at lunchtime instead of seven, and on a busy night she can write one report, not three.
options.senior: One agent and a person is cheaper per report and easier to check, and for questions that don't split it is usually the better tool. On wide questions with independent parts, it reads fewer sources and takes longer, and the person becomes the bottleneck, the one slow point everything waits on. Keep it for the questions that need it.

sim.title: Rerun Tuesday's report through the circle
sim.lede: You're Nunzia at 23:00 on Tuesday, before the lead hands anything out. No real model runs: each agent follows stated rules over stated data. Wrayholme's question has four parts (ports, money, decisions, ferry lines), and each part, done by one worker, has a stated cost in tokens, minutes and sources read. With one-line briefs the lead gives worker 1 the first part, worker 2 the second and so on, counting round again when there are more workers than parts, and the line for ferry lines has no UK only unless you add it. With full briefs, each part gets one worker and a brief with an objective, limits and an output format; spare workers aren't started. The lead plans for 3 minutes and merges for 6; workers run at the same time. By the sim's merge rule, notes with no source on them are merged by the lead, which joins two notes about shore power with the same date into one event. Workers messaging each other read every other worker's notes as extra tokens and wait 5 more minutes. One agent is the firm's own run with a single agent. Prices are the firm's invoice, $3 a million tokens in and $15 out. The second question, one thread, is Thursday's follow-up: how Inchcombe decided, step by step.
sim.tryThis: Try this: run it as built, five workers and one-line briefs. 7 claims, the meeting from workers 3 and 4, a Norwegian claim, worker 5 repeating worker 1, 958,000 tokens in, $3.47, 3.8 times one agent. Tick one agent: $0.92, 58 minutes, nothing invented, 6 claims. Go to eight workers: 4 duplicated subtasks, the meeting still there, $5.41. Back to five and write UK only into every line: no meeting, the duplicate still there. Let the workers message each other: the meeting is now in 2 workers' own notes, $3.83. Switch to full briefs: 8 claims, nothing invented or repeated, $2.86. Then pick the one-thread question and compare the circle with one agent.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at the table made up a meeting. The lead agent handed out one-line jobs, one without UK only and two the same. Then it joined notes that said nothing about where they came from, so two true notes with the same date became one false event.

steps.title: The circle is a lead and its workers.
steps.text: Anthropic's guide Building effective agents calls the pattern orchestrator-workers: a central LLM dynamically breaks down tasks, delegates them to worker LLMs, and synthesizes their results. (An LLM, a large language model, is the kind of model behind each agent; an orchestrator is the one in charge, like a conductor; to synthesize is to combine.) Garthwick's lead is the planner. A run goes in steps. First the lead reads the whole question and splits it into subtasks; if it splits badly, parts overlap or go missing. Second, it writes one handoff per worker; anything it leaves out, the worker never learns. Third, each worker, a sub-agent with its own context window (the most text a model holds at once), searches and reads on its own. Fourth, the workers send notes back; a note with no source can't be checked. Last, the lead merges the notes into one report, and that is where notes that don't belong together can get joined. Because the workers run at the same time, Tuesday's run took 26 minutes where one agent, searching one thing after another, took 58.

steps.title: Every handoff is a brief, and one line loses things.
steps.text: The instructions that go with a handoff are called a brief. A worker knows only its brief, the way a temp knows only the note left on the desk. The client's question said UK. Worker 4's line said ferry lines, so it read eight Norwegian sources. Workers 1 and 5 got the same line and read the same nine. Anthropic's research team (subagent is their word for a worker) met the same thing: with short instructions like research the semiconductor shortage, one subagent explored the 2021 automotive chip crisis while 2 others duplicated work. Their rule: each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries.

steps.title: The lead owns the shared notes, and every note carries its source.
steps.text: The workers' notes came back as paragraphs with no worker and no source on them, and the lead wrote from one pasted file. Two true notes shared a date and a topic, and the merge joined them into one event, the same failure as merging two people by name without checking. An output format is the shape a worker's result must take. With one finding a line, each with its source link, date and place, the lead keeps each finding apart and can check any of them. Anthropic's system ends with a citation step, a last pass that points each claim at its source, so all claims are properly attributed to their sources.

steps.title: Many hands cost many times.
steps.text: Anthropic reports that its multi-agent system outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on its internal research eval (its own test of research questions with known answers), and that agents use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions (one plain question and answer), multi-agent systems about 15× more. Every worker reads its own sources into its own context window, and all of it is billed. Garthwick's run used 998,000 tokens against one agent's 250,000, $3.47 against $0.92, 3.8 times. With full briefs it was $2.86, still 3.1 times, and it found both of Thurloe's answers that one agent missed. Pay that only where the question is worth it.

steps.title: When one agent is better.
steps.text: The same post says domains that require all agents to share the same context or involve many dependencies between agents are not a good fit for multi-agent systems today. Thursday's follow-up, how Inchcombe decided step by step, is one thread: each step rests on the last, so no part can be researched apart. Split it and you pay for the lead and get nothing back: $0.72 against one agent's $0.44, the same 3 claims. Workers messaging each other doesn't fix this either; in the sim it put the meeting into two workers' own notes.

diagram.aria: The fix. The client's question, four parts, UK only, goes to the lead agent, which writes four full briefs and keeps the shared notes, where every finding has a claim, a source link, a date and a place. The lead hands one brief each to four workers: ports, money, decisions and ferry lines, each with UK only, 2022 on. Each reports back to the lead. Tuesday's rerun: 8 claims, none invented, none duplicated, $2.86, 26 minutes. A question that doesn't split goes to one agent.

notes.text: Each worker reports back to the lead, never to each other.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for tonight. The lead writes one full brief per part of the question, with an objective, limits and an output format, so no two workers share a part and every worker carries UK only. Workers hand their findings back to the lead, one finding a line with its source, and the lead keeps the shared notes. A question that is one thread goes to one agent instead.

fix.title: The fix: full briefs, notes the lead owns, and one agent when the question doesn't split
fix.text: Have the lead write every handoff as a brief, not a line: the objective (what this worker must find), the limits (UK ports only, January 2022 on, public sources), the output format (one finding a line, with claim, source link, date and place) and the sources to start from. One brief per part, so no two workers share one; a spare worker isn't started. Workers report only to the lead, and the lead keeps the shared notes as findings each marked with its worker and source, merging only findings that cite the same source and leaving the rest as separate claims. Before splitting a question, the lead asks whether its parts can be researched apart; one thread, where each step rests on the last, goes to one agent. Log every brief and every finding with the worker that wrote it, so a reader can trace any sentence back to a page.

limits: Full briefs only carry what the lead puts in them. A limit missing from the client's question, or one the lead misreads, goes to every worker; someone still checks the briefs against the question.
A source on every finding makes checking possible, not done. A worker can cite a real page that doesn't say what the note claims, so sample findings against their pages before a report goes out.

The circle with full briefs still cost 3.1 times one agent on Tuesday's question. That is worth it for wide questions a client pays for, and wasteful for narrow ones; the lead has to decide which it has, and can get that wrong.

explain.seniorTake: A lead and workers buy breadth and speed on questions that split into parts you can research apart, and you pay for it in tokens, usually several times one agent. Most of what goes wrong happens at the handoffs: a worker knows only its brief, and the lead knows only what comes back. So write every brief with an objective, limits and an output format, keep one set of notes with a source on every finding, and keep a single agent for work that is one thread.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: a lead and subagents beat one agent on research, June 2025
realWorld.text: In How we built our multi-agent research system, Anthropic's team says a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on our internal research eval. Their example was being asked to identify all the board members of the companies in the Information Technology S&P 500 (a list of 500 large US companies, sorted by industry): the multi-agent system split the work, and the single agent system failed to find the answer with slow, sequential searches (one after another).

realWorld.title: Anthropic: what it costs in tokens
realWorld.text: The same post says agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats. It found that token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance (how much the scores differed) in its evaluation, and says that for economic viability, multi-agent systems require tasks where the value of the task is high enough to pay for the increased performance. Its prompts scale effort to the question: simple fact-finding requires just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls (uses of a tool).

realWorld.title: Anthropic: short briefs duplicated work
realWorld.text: The team started by allowing the lead agent to give simple, short instructions like research the semiconductor shortage, and found one subagent explored the 2021 automotive chip crisis while 2 others duplicated work. Without detailed task descriptions, agents duplicate work, leave gaps, or fail to find necessary information. Its rule: each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: where many agents are worse
realWorld.text: The post says some domains that require all agents to share the same context or involve many dependencies between agents are not a good fit for multi-agent systems today. Most coding tasks involve fewer truly parallelizable tasks (ones that can run at the same time) than research, and LLM agents are not yet great at coordinating and delegating to other agents in real time. Its lead agents execute subagents synchronously (waiting for each batch to finish), so the lead can't steer subagents, subagents can't coordinate, and the entire system can be blocked.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: notes outside the window, a source for every claim
realWorld.text: In the same system the lead begins by saving its plan to Memory (storage outside its context window) to persist the context, since a context window over 200,000 tokens will be truncated (cut off). Subagents call tools to store their work in external systems, then pass lightweight references (short pointers, such as a file name) back to the coordinator (the lead). At the end the findings go to a CitationAgent (an agent that adds the sources), which processes the documents and research report to identify specific locations for citations, so all claims are properly attributed to their sources.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: the pattern's name, December 2024
realWorld.text: Building effective agents says that in the orchestrator-workers workflow, a central LLM dynamically breaks down tasks, delegates them to worker LLMs, and synthesizes their results, and that it is well-suited for complex tasks where you can't predict the subtasks needed.

asked: When is a multi-agent system worth it?
How should an orchestrator brief its workers?
What goes wrong in agent handoffs?
interview.answer: A multi-agent system is worth it when the task splits into parts that can be researched apart, the breadth matters, and the task is valuable enough to pay several times the tokens of one agent; Anthropic reports multi-agent systems use about 15 times the tokens of chat against about 4 times for one agent. When the parts depend on each other or need the same context, one agent is usually better and cheaper. The orchestrator, the lead agent, should write each worker a brief, not a line: the objective, the limits such as country, dates and allowed sources, the output format, ideally one finding a line with its source, and the boundaries that keep it off another worker's ground. Workers report back to the orchestrator, which owns the shared notes and merges only findings it can trace. What goes wrong at handoffs is loss: a constraint that never reaches a worker, two workers given the same task, a gap nobody covers, and notes that come back without their sources, so the merge joins things that don't belong together. I log every brief and every finding with its worker and source, and measure the system against one agent on the same questions for quality, cost and time.

Electricity from the land supplied to a ship at its berth, so it can switch off its engines in port.
A place in a port where a ship ties up. A shore power berth has the cables and equipment to plug a ship in.
The official in charge of a port's harbour: its ships, berths and safety. Hilary Sowerby is Inchcombe's.
The group that runs a port and decides its spending, recorded in minutes. Inchcombe's minutes are kept by Tregenza.
A company that runs ferries on set routes. Wrayholme Ferries is the client; Havbrua is a Norwegian line.
The written record of a meeting: who was there, what was decided and when.
Several agents working on one job, each a model going round its own loop of read, decide, act. Like a crew with a foreman. Here, a lead agent and its workers.
The agent that reads the whole job, splits it into subtasks, hands them out, and merges what comes back. Anthropic calls it the orchestrator or lead; here it is the planner.
The part of a system that decides how to split a job and who does each piece. In the circle, the lead agent.
An agent given one subtask by the lead. It is a sub-agent: its own context window (the most text it can hold), its own searches, and a result it hands back.
One piece of the client's question given to one worker, such as which UK ports committed money to shore power since 2022.
The moment work passes from one agent to another, and what goes with it. A worker knows only what its handoff says.
The instructions that go with a subtask. Tuesday's were one line each.
A subtask given as a single sentence, such as find which ferry lines will plug in to shore power. It leaves out whatever the lead didn't think to write.
A brief with an objective, limits and an output format, and sources to start from. In the sim, one per part of the question.
What a worker must find, stated so it can tell when it is done.
The boundaries of a subtask: country, dates, allowed sources, and what belongs to another worker. Tuesday's question had two, UK only and since 2022; worker 4's line lost the first.
The shape a worker's result must take. Here, one finding a line: claim, source link, date and place.
Everything the workers hand back, kept in one place the lead writes from. Tuesday's were one scratch file of pasted paragraphs.
What several agents read and write in common while working on one job. In the circle, the shared notes.
Another name for the lead agent, used in Anthropic's post.
Storage outside the context window (the most text a model holds at once) where Anthropic's lead agent saves its plan, so the plan survives if the window is cut off.
A stone or concrete platform along the water where ships tie up and load.
One fact a worker reports, such as a date of a decision. In a full brief, each finding carries its source.
The lead's last step: turning the shared notes into one report. With no sources on the notes, it can join things that don't belong together.
The sim's stated rule: notes with no source are merged by joining two notes about shore power with the same date into one event. Findings marked with a source stay apart.
A subtask given to a second worker when another already has it. Worker 5's repeated worker 1's and read the same nine sources.
A part of the question no worker was given, so the report says nothing about it.
One agent doing the whole job in one context, searching one thing after another. The firm's comparison run.
At the same time. The circle's workers run in parallel, so the run takes as long as the slowest one plus the lead's time.
A question whose steps depend on each other, such as how one port decided step by step, so it doesn't split into parts researched apart.
The worker whose line said ferry lines with no UK only. It read eight Norwegian sources, including Havbrua's.
An upturned glass that everyone at a séance touches with a finger; it slides to letters to spell a message, and nobody owns the push. Like the pointer on a talking board.
A working file the lead pasted every worker's notes into and wrote the report from. Nothing in it said who wrote what.
Workers reading each other's notes as they work. In the sim each reads every other's notes as extra input, and the run waits 5 more minutes.
Another name for the lead agent: the model in charge of splitting the work and combining the results.
Anthropic's word for the workers in its research system, each searching at the same time as the others and reporting back to the lead.
Anthropic's internal test of research questions with known answers, used to compare its multi-agent system with one agent.
One of Anthropic's Claude models, released in 2025, used as both the lead and the single agent in its comparison.
One ordinary exchange with a chat assistant: a question and an answer, with no tools or loop. Anthropic's baseline for token use.
How much results differ from run to run or question to question. Anthropic found token use alone explained 80% of it in its evaluation.
Whether something pays for itself. Anthropic says multi-agent systems need tasks valuable enough to cover their extra tokens.
One after another, each waiting for the last. Anthropic's lead waits for each set of subagents to finish before going on.
The last agent in Anthropic's research system: it reads the documents and the report and marks where each claim's source is.
A list of 500 large US companies, grouped by sector. Information Technology is one sector.
One of the directors who oversee a company or a port, voting on its big decisions.
Able to be split into parts that run at the same time without waiting for each other.
A short pointer, such as a file name, passed instead of the whole result, so the lead's context stays small.
Cut off. Text beyond a context window's limit is dropped, which is why Anthropic's lead saves its plan outside it.
Large language model: a program trained on huge amounts of writing to read and write text. It is the kind of model behind each agent here.
People who check a company carefully before a deal, such as a purchase or an investment, and write up what they find.
Two statements that can't both be true, such as two summaries giving a company different owners.
A piece of work handed to a client as part of a service, such as a report.
Documents a company must file with a public registry, such as its accounts and who owns and runs it.
A company that exists to own shares in other companies.
Digging silt from the bottom of a harbour or channel so ships can get in.
ISO 9001's term for information an organisation must keep in writing and control, such as procedures, briefs and records.
Able to be followed back to where it came from: here, each sentence to its finding, worker and source page.

atWork: Look for places where your systems hand one job to several agents or model calls and then stitch the results together. A common incident: a due-diligence team, people who check a company before a deal, ran three agents over the company's filings (the papers it must lodge with a public registry), news and contracts, each told in one line to summarise the company. The three summaries overlapped by most of their length, and there was one contradiction: one said the company's owner was a holding firm (a company that exists to own others) the other two never mentioned; nobody could say which source it came from. Write down, for each handoff, exactly what the receiving agent is told, and check it carries the client's limits. Make every result come back in a fixed shape with a source on each finding, keep the merged notes in one place, and run the same questions through one agent to compare quality, cost and time before deciding the extra agents are worth it. Standards-readiness note: if these reports are deliverables, work handed to clients, at a firm that holds or is pursuing ISO 9001:2015 certification, clause 8.5.1 asks that service provision happen under controlled conditions, including documented information that defines the results to be achieved; briefs written down with their limits and output format, and findings traceable to their sources, are much easier to show as controlled than one-line handoffs and an untagged scratch file. Build it in now rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your team's research assistant splits each question among four sub-agents, giving each a one-sentence instruction. Reports keep coming back with two sub-agents covering the same ground, and last week one quoted figures from the wrong year. What do you change in how the lead hands out work, and in what comes back?

keyIdeas.idea: Each brief states an objective and clear boundaries, so no two sub-agents share ground
The limits from the question (dates, country, sources) are written into every brief
An output format with a source on each finding, so the lead can check and merge them

recall.model: Stop sending one sentence. Have the lead write each sub-agent a brief: an objective that says what it must find and when it is done, boundaries that say what belongs to the others so no two cover the same ground, and the limits from the question, here the year range, written into every brief rather than left in the user's question. Ask for a fixed output format: one finding a line, with its source link and date. The lead keeps those findings in one place and merges only what it can trace, so a figure from the wrong year shows its source and gets caught before the report goes out.

recall.prompt: Why did Tuesday's report say Hilary Sowerby and Ragnhild Skjelbred met at the Inchcombe harbour office?
options: One worker made the meeting up because its model invents things more than the others
The lead merged two true notes with the same date and no source, one from a worker that never got UK only
Two workers researched the same part, and their notes disagreed
Havbrua's press release said the meeting happened, and worker 4 copied it
recall.why: Both notes were true: Sowerby announced Inchcombe's funding at the harbour office on 14 March 2024, and Skjelbred signed a deal on a quay in Brennvika the same day. Worker 4 read Norwegian sources because its line said ferry lines with no UK only. Neither note carried a source or a worker, so the merge joined them into one event. The duplicated work, workers 1 and 5, was a separate waste.

recall.prompt: Which of these jobs is most likely better done by one agent than by a lead with four workers?
options: Listing the board members of fifty separate companies
Comparing the prices of the same product at twenty shops
Tracing how one council reached one decision, step by step, where each step explains the next
Summarising news about four unrelated industries for a weekly digest
recall.why: A step-by-step trace is one thread: each step depends on the last, so the parts can't be researched apart and every worker would need the same context. Anthropic's post says tasks with many dependencies between agents, or that need all agents to share the same context, are not a good fit for multi-agent systems today. The other three split into independent parts, which is where a lead and workers earn their extra tokens.

recall.prompt: Your product's single research agent takes about 50 minutes per report. A colleague proposes rebuilding it as a lead with six parallel sub-agents, because it will be faster and more thorough. How do you decide, and what would you measure?

keyIdeas.idea: It costs several times the tokens of one agent, so the task must be valuable enough to pay for it
Only worth it if the reports split into independent parts; one-thread work stays with one agent
Run both on the same set of real questions and compare quality, cost and time

recall.model: Decide on evidence. A lead with workers usually costs several times the tokens of one agent; Anthropic reports about 15 times chat for multi-agent systems against about 4 times for one agent, so the reports must be worth that. Look at the questions first: if most split into parts that can be researched independently, parallel workers can be faster and cover more; if most are one thread, where each step depends on the last, keep one agent. Then run both versions on the same set of real questions with agreed answers, and compare claims that check out, gaps, invented claims, cost per report and minutes per report.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. Full briefs fixed the circle: every finding has its source, and nothing has been invented since. Now Ms Nesbitt wants the circle on a new kind of job, a timeline for a client: how one harbour's dredging decision (digging silt off the harbour floor so ships can get in) moved from first proposal to contract, where each meeting refers back to the one before. Her plan is five workers, one per year, with full briefs, plus letting the workers message each other so each year can see what happened in the last.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Is the circle the right tool for this job, and what would you do?

keyIdeas.idea: It is one thread: each step depends on the one before, so it doesn't split into independent parts
Use one agent for it, which costs less and keeps the whole story in one context
Workers messaging each other spreads unchecked notes and costs more; the lead should own the notes

coldCase.model: No. A timeline where each meeting refers back to the one before is one thread: the steps depend on each other, so splitting it by year gives five workers who each need the others' context. Anthropic's post names exactly this, tasks that need all agents to share the same context or have many dependencies between agents, as a poor fit for multi-agent systems today. Letting the workers message each other doesn't fix it; it spreads each worker's unchecked notes to the rest and adds tokens, and nobody owns the result. Give this job to one agent, with a full brief and the same output format, one finding a line with its source, so the whole story sits in one context and every step can be checked. Keep the circle for wide questions with parts that can be researched apart.

sources.title: Jeremy Hadfield, Barry Zhang, Kenneth Lien, Florian Scholz, Jeremy Fox and Daniel Ford, How we built our multi-agent research system, Anthropic Engineering, published 13 June 2025, read 11 October 2026: a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on our internal research eval; agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats; token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance; each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries; one subagent explored the 2021 automotive chip crisis while 2 others duplicated work; domains that require all agents to share the same context or involve many dependencies between agents are not a good fit

Erik S. and Barry Zhang, Building effective agents, Anthropic Engineering, published 19 December 2024, read 11 October 2026: in the orchestrator-workers workflow, a central LLM dynamically breaks down tasks, delegates them to worker LLMs, and synthesizes their results; well-suited for complex tasks where you can't predict the subtasks needed
